zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

headline: Tough Grind, Better Read: The 100-Fathom Edge Bailed Out a Slow Week South
subhead: Four canyons, one warm pool that won't move — here's where it actually paid to run this week.
body_markdown:
Call it a C-plus week with a strong finish. Monday through Wednesday I burned diesel running between Spencer and Lindenkohl looking for the kind of green, clean water we had in July, and mostly what I found was empty ocean and a slick of bait that never held together long enough to matter. By Thursday the picture changed — not because the fish came back to the deep lumps everybody wants to run to, but because we finally figured out where they'd gone: shallower, onto the shelf itself, sitting the 100-fathom line instead of pushing all the way out to the thousand-fathom structure this fleet's been trained to chase since June.

That's the story of the whole southern stretch right now. The warm pool that's been parked over this water since early August hasn't moved much, but it's pushed the most productive edge up onto the shelf. You could see it in the results out of Ocean City — 334 boats fished six days of the White Marlin Open and the fleet only put three bigeyes on the dock. That's not a fleet that forgot how to fish. That's a fleet that ran to the same grounds that have produced for years and found them dead, because the water that usually sits over those lumps has slid inshore on them.

Here's how I worked it. Spencer first — I like Spencer early in any pattern shift because the canyon head sits close enough to the shelf edge that if the warm water's crawling shallow, Spencer feels it before Norfolk does. We worked the 100-fathom curve on the northeast wall Thursday, trolling a standard spread of ballyhoo behind cedar plugs with a couple green machines out the long riggers, hunting the temperature break instead of the bottom contour like we normally would. Marked scattered yellowfin on the troll that afternoon, mixed with a few gaffer mahi holding under a scrap of floating grass we ran into with actual bait under it. Nothing that filled a box in an hour, but enough bites to confirm the fish were there — just thin and moving, not stacked.

Lindenkohl was the disappointment of the week. Ran up there Tuesday expecting the same edge water that's carried us all summer and instead found a flat, dead push with almost no life past the drop-off on the meter. If you're planning a Lindenkohl trip this week, I'd hold off until somebody confirms that edge has re-formed. No sense burning the extra run for water that looked the way it did Tuesday.

Poor Man's is the canyon I keep coming back to because it's the shortest run and it's been the most forgiving when the bite gets choosy like this. We chunked butterfish over structure inside the canyon head Thursday night into Friday morning and picked at yellowfin in the 20-to-35-pound class, plus one respectable bigeye that came up in the chum slick around midnight. That's your night bite — with the warm pool sitting where it is, the bigeye pattern favors after-dark chunking over daytime trolling right now. Squid strips and butterfish chunks both drew fish, but butterfish held them in the slick longer.

Norfolk's the wild card because it's far enough south that it reads the warm pool differently than the other three, and this week that worked in our favor. One boat reported a wahoo on a high-speed spread — bird teaser up front, cedar plugs and a diving lure running planers around 14 knots along the shelf break south of the canyon. That's the first legitimate wahoo chatter I've had out of this zone all month, and it lines up with something we flagged a few days back — that the warm pool holding its position into mid-August would eventually start pulling wahoo up onto these edges. One fish doesn't make a run, but it's the kind of early signal worth watching if you're plotting your next trip south.

White marlin have been quiet across all four canyons — a couple of respectable bites on naked ballyhoo behind Sea Witches trolled over Poor Man's, but nothing consistent enough to call a pattern yet. Same story with bluefin. The water's simply too warm right now for them to hold anywhere but the deepest, coldest pockets, and those pockets have been hard to pin down this week.

If I had one day to fish this weekend, I'd run to Poor Man's for the night chunk bite and stage close enough to slide over to Spencer's shelf edge at first light if the overnight report comes back soft. The moon's building toward the August 28 full, which should tighten the tide and concentrate bait better than the slack water we've been fighting. If that warm pool holds its current position through the weekend, expect the shelf-edge pattern at Spencer and Norfolk to keep outproducing the deep water everybody's used to running. If it slides back offshore, the deep grounds could turn back on fast — that's the single biggest variable I'm watching heading into next week, and I'll be checking it every morning before I decide which canyon gets the first run.
